Others said that it refers to the content and the sciences it contains. The sciences of the Qur'an are three: tawhid (the oneness of God), ahkam (legal rulings), and qasas (narratives). This surah includes tawhid, so it is a third of the Qur'an in this respect. This is the more apparent view, and Ibn 'Atiyya interpreted the hadith accordingly. This is supported by some versions of the hadith, which say: "God divided the Qur'an into three parts and made ﴿Say: He is God, the One﴾ one of its parts." Al-Nasa'i reported that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) heard a man reciting it and said: "This one has been forgiven." In another narration he said: "Paradise has become obligatory for him." Muslim reported that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) sent a man at the head of a military detachment, and he used to recite ﴿Say: He is God, the One﴾ to his companions in the prayer. When they returned, they mentioned this to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), who said: "Ask him why he does this." They asked him, and he said: "Because it is the attribute of the Most Merciful, so I love to recite it." The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Inform him that God loves him." In a narration transmitted by al-Tirmidhi, he (ﷺ) said to the man: "Your love for it has admitted you into Paradise." Al-Tirmidhi also reported that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Whoever recites ﴿Say: He is God, the One﴾ one hundred times every day, his sins for fifty years will be forgiven, unless he has a debt."

﴿Say: He is God, the One﴾. The pronoun here, according to the Basrans, is the pronoun of the matter and the affair (ḍamīr al-amr wa al-sha'n), used to express glorification and magnification. Its i'rab (grammatical analysis) is that it is a subject (mubtada'), and its predicate is the clause that follows it, which explains it. "God" is the subject and "One" (aḥad) is the predicate. It was also said: "God" is the predicate and "One" is an appositive (badal) for it. It was also said: "God" is an appositive, and "One" is the predicate. Aḥad has two meanings. One is that it is among the words of negation, which occur only in non-affirmative contexts, as in your saying: "No one came to me." This is not the place for that meaning; its place is His saying: ﴿and there is none comparable to Him﴾. The other is that it means "one," and its origin is waḥid with a waw, which was then replaced by a hamza. This is the meaning intended here.

Know that describing God Most High as Wahid (the One) has three meanings, all of which are correct with respect to God Most High. First: He is One with no second with Him, so it is a negation of number. Second: He is One with no equal and no partner, as you say: "So-and-so is the unique one of his age," meaning he has no equal. Third: He is One who is not divisible and has no parts. The more apparent view is that what is meant in the surah is the negation of a partner, with the intent of refuting the polytheists. From this is His saying: ﴿And your God is one God﴾ [al-Baqarah: 163]. Al-Zamakhshari said: "Aḥad is an attribute of unity and the negation of partners." I say: God has established in the Qur'an decisive proofs of His oneness, and these are very numerous in the Qur'an. The clearest of them are four proofs. The first is His saying: ﴿Is then He who creates like one who does not create?﴾ [al-Naḥl: 17], for when it is established that God is the Creator of all existing things, it is impossible for any of them to be His partner. The second is His saying: ﴿If there had been in them gods other than God, they would have been ruined﴾ [al-Anbiyā': 22]. The third is His saying: ﴿Say: If there had been with Him gods as they say, they would have sought a way to the Possessor of the Throne﴾ [al-Isrā': 42]. The fourth is His saying: ﴿And there was not with Him any god; otherwise, each god would have taken away what he created, and some of them would have overcome others﴾ [al-Mu'minūn: 91]. We have explained these verses in their places, and we have discussed the reality of tawhid (oneness of God) in His saying: ﴿And your God is one God﴾ [al-Baqarah: 163].

﴿God, the Eternal Refuge﴾. There are three opinions concerning the meaning of al-ṣamad (the Eternal Refuge). The first: al-ṣamad is the one to whom one turns in affairs, that is, one who is sought for refuge. The second: He neither eats nor drinks, as in His saying: ﴿He feeds but is not fed﴾ [al-An'ām: 14]. The third: He has no hollow interior. The first is what is meant here according to the more apparent view. Ibn 'Atiyya preferred it, because God is the originator of existing things and by Him they subsist. They are in need of Him, that is, they turn to Him, since they cannot subsist by themselves. Our shaykh, the professor Abū Ja'far ibn al-Zubayr, also preferred it, because this meaning occurs in the Qur'an wherever the negation of offspring from God is mentioned, as in His saying concerning Maryam: ﴿And they say: God has taken a son﴾, followed by His saying: ﴿There is none in the heavens and the earth but that he comes to the Most Merciful as a servant﴾ [Maryam: 93]; and His saying: ﴿The Originator of the heavens and the earth: how could He have a son?﴾ [al-An'ām: 101]; and His saying: ﴿And they say: God has taken a son. Glory be to Him! Rather, to Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth﴾ [al-Baqarah: 116]. Likewise, it is mentioned here together with His saying ﴿He neither begets nor is begotten﴾, as a proof for the negation of offspring. Al-Zamakhshari said: ṣamad is of the form faʻal in the sense of mafʻūl (passive), because He is the one sought in needs.

﴿He neither begets nor is begotten﴾. This is a refutation of everyone who attributed a son to God: the Christians, in their saying "Jesus is the son of God"; the Jews, in their saying "Ezra is the son of God"; and the Arabs, in their saying "the angels are the daughters of God." God has established proofs in the Qur'an for the negation of offspring, and the clearest of them are four arguments. The first: a son must necessarily be of the same kind as his father, and God has no kind, so it is impossible for Him to have a son. To this the reference is in His saying: ﴿The Messiah, son of Maryam, was not but a messenger; messengers had passed on before him, and his mother was a woman of truth; they both used to eat food﴾ [al-Mā'idah: 75]. He described them with the attribute of createdness in order to negate from them the attribute of eternity, and thus the claim of the disbelievers is nullified. The second: a father takes a son only because of need for him, and God has no need of anything, so He does not take a son. To this He refers in His saying: ﴿They say: God has taken a son. Glory be to Him; He is the Self-Sufficient﴾ [Yūnus: 68]. The third: all creation are servants of God, and servanthood contradicts being a begotten son. To this He refers in His saying: ﴿There is none in the heavens and the earth but that he comes to the Most Merciful as a servant﴾ [Maryam: 93]. The fourth: one can have a son only if one has a wife, and God has not taken a wife, so He cannot have a son. To this refers His saying: ﴿How can He have a son when He has no companion?﴾ [al-An'ām: 101].

﴿And He was not begotten﴾. This is a refutation of those who said: "Describe your Lord to us [by lineage]." Every begotten thing is originated, whereas God Most High is the First, whose existence has no beginning, the Eternal who was and nothing was with Him other than Himself. It is therefore impossible that He be begotten, exalted is He above that.

﴿Nor is there to Him any equivalent — anyone﴾. The kufu' (equivalent) is the peer and the like. Al-Zamakhshari said: it may be taken from kafā'ah (compatibility) in marriage, so that it would be a negation of a spouse. This is far-fetched, and the first meaning is the correct one: that God has no peer, no resemblance, and no likeness. In kufuwan it is permitted to pronounce the fā' with a ḍamma or with a sukūn, with the kāf having a ḍamma. It has been read in both ways. It is also permitted to pronounce the kāf with a kasra and the fā' with a sukūn, and to pronounce the kāf with a kasra and the fā' with a fatḥa and the long vowel. It is also permitted to pronounce it with a hamza or with tas-hīl (softening of the hamza). Kufuwan is in the accusative as the predicate of kāna (was), and aḥad is its subject. Ibn 'Atiyya said: it is also permitted that kufuwan be its ḥāl (circumstantial accusative), since it was originally an attribute of an indefinite noun and was then placed before it. If it is asked: why was the prepositional phrase lahu (to Him), which is not the predicate, placed before the subject of kāna and its predicate, when the rule is that an adverbial phrase, when not the predicate, is postponed? The answer has two aspects. First, it was placed first for emphasis and magnification, because it refers to God Most High, and it is the custom of the Arabs to place first what is more important and more appropriate. Second, this prepositional phrase completes the meaning of the predicate and fulfills its function, since the intent is not the general negation of any equal but the negation of an equal from God Most High. For this reason the prepositional phrase that secures this meaning was given attention and placed first.

If it is asked: His saying ﴿Say: He is God, the One﴾ already implies the negation of offspring and of an equal, so why was this explicitly stated after it? The answer: this is from al-tajrīd (singling out), which is the specification of a thing by mention after it has already been included in the generality of what preceded, as in His saying: ﴿His angels and His messengers, and Jibrīl and Mikā'īl﴾ [al-Baqarah: 98]. This is done for two reasons, each of which is valid here. The first is attentiveness: there is no doubt that the negation of offspring and of an equal from God deserves attention, in refutation of those among the disbelievers who say otherwise. The second is clarification and explanation, for the inclusion of a matter within a general statement is not like its explicit mention. So this was stated explicitly for clarification and elucidation of the meaning, for emphasis in refuting the disbelievers, and for confirming the proof against them.

Glory be to Him; He is the Self-Sufficient﴾ [Yūnus: 68]. The third: all creation are servants of God, and servanthood contradicts being a begotten son. To this He refers in His saying: ﴿There is none in the heavens and the earth but that he comes to the Most Merciful as a servant﴾ [Maryam: 93]. The fourth: one can have a son only if one has a wife, and God has not taken a wife, so He cannot have a son. To this refers His saying: ﴿How can He have a son when He has no companion?﴾ [al-An'ām: 101].

﴿And He was not begotten﴾. This is a refutation of those who said: "Describe your Lord to us [by lineage]." Every begotten thing is originated, whereas God Most High is the First, whose existence has no beginning, the Eternal who was and nothing was with Him other than Himself. It is therefore impossible that He be begotten, exalted is He above that.

﴿Nor is there to Him any equivalent — anyone﴾. The kufu' (equivalent) is the peer and the like. Al-Zamakhshari said: it may be taken from kafā'ah (compatibility) in marriage, so that it would be a negation of a spouse. This is far-fetched, and the first meaning is the correct one: that God has no peer, no resemblance, and no likeness. In kufuwan it is permitted to pronounce the fā' with a ḍamma or with a sukūn, with the kāf having a ḍamma. It has been read in both ways. It is also permitted to pronounce the kāf with a kasra and the fā' with a sukūn, and to pronounce the kāf with a kasra and the fā' with a fatḥa and the long vowel. It is also permitted to pronounce it with a hamza or with tas-hīl (softening of the hamza). Kufuwan is in the accusative as the predicate of kāna (was), and aḥad is its subject. The answer has two aspects. First, it was placed first for emphasis and magnification, because it refers to God Most High, and it is the custom of the Arabs to place first what is more important and more appropriate. Second, this prepositional phrase completes the meaning of the predicate and fulfills its function, since the intent is not the general negation of any equal but the negation of an equal from God Most High. For this reason the prepositional phrase that secures this meaning was given attention and placed first.

If it is asked: His saying ﴿Say: He is God, the One﴾ already implies the negation of offspring and of an equal, so why was this explicitly stated after it? The answer: this is from al-tajrīd (singling out), which is the specification of a thing by mention after it has already been included in the generality of what preceded, as in His saying: ﴿His angels and His messengers, and Jibrīl and Mikā'īl﴾ [al-Baqarah: 98]. This is done for two reasons, each of which is valid here. The first is attentiveness: there is no doubt that the negation of offspring and of an equal from God deserves attention, in refutation of those among the disbelievers who say otherwise. The second is clarification and explanation, for the inclusion of a matter within a general statement is not like its explicit mention. So this was stated explicitly for clarification and elucidation of the meaning, for emphasis in refuting the disbelievers, and for confirming the proof against them.

Ibn Juzayy's commentary on Surah 112, verses 1–4 (al-Tashil)

Scholars have differed over the meaning of the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying about ﴿Say: He is God, the One﴾ that it is "equal to a third of the Qur'an." Some said that this refers to the reward: whoever recites it receives a reward equal to that of one who recites a third of the Qur'an. Others said that it refers to the content and the sciences it contains. The sciences of the Qur'an are three: tawhid (the oneness of God), ahkam (legal rulings), and qasas (narratives). This surah includes tawhid, so it is a third of the Qur'an in this respect. This is the more apparent view, and Ibn 'Atiyya interpreted the hadith accordingly. This is supported by some versions of the hadith, which say: "God divided the Qur'an into three parts and made ﴿Say: He is God, the One﴾ one of its parts." Al-Nasa'i reported that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) heard a man reciting it and said: "This one has been forgiven." In another narration he said: "Paradise has become obligatory for him." Muslim reported that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) sent a man at the head of a military detachment, and he used to recite ﴿Say: He is God, the One﴾ to his companions in the prayer. When they returned, they mentioned this to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), who said: "Ask him why he does this." They asked him, and he said: "Because it is the attribute of the Most Merciful, so I love to recite it." The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Inform him that God loves him." In a narration transmitted by al-Tirmidhi, he (ﷺ) said to the man: "Your love for it has admitted you into Paradise." Al-Tirmidhi also reported that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Whoever recites ﴿Say: He is God, the One﴾ one hundred times every day, his sins for fifty years will be forgiven, unless he has a debt."

﴿Say: He is God, the One﴾. The pronoun here, according to the Basrans, is the pronoun of the matter and the affair (ḍamīr al-amr wa al-sha'n), used to express glorification and magnification. Its i'rab (grammatical analysis) is that it is a subject (mubtada'), and its predicate is the clause that follows it, which explains it. "God" is the subject and "One" (aḥad) is the predicate. It was also said: "God" is the predicate and "One" is an appositive (badal) for it. It was also said: "God" is an appositive, and "One" is the predicate. Aḥad has two meanings. One is that it is among the words of negation, which occur only in non-affirmative contexts, as in your saying: "No one came to me." This is not the place for that meaning; its place is His saying: ﴿and there is none comparable to Him﴾. The other is that it means "one," and its origin is waḥid with a waw, which was then replaced by a hamza. This is the meaning intended here.

Know that describing God Most High as Wahid (the One) has three meanings, all of which are correct with respect to God Most High. First: He is One with no second with Him, so it is a negation of number. Second: He is One with no equal and no partner, as you say: "So-and-so is the unique one of his age," meaning he has no equal. Third: He is One who is not divisible and has no parts. The more apparent view is that what is meant in the surah is the negation of a partner, with the intent of refuting the polytheists. From this is His saying: ﴿And your God is one God﴾ [al-Baqarah: 163]. Al-Zamakhshari said: "Aḥad is an attribute of unity and the negation of partners." I say: God has established in the Qur'an decisive proofs of His oneness, and these are very numerous in the Qur'an. The clearest of them are four proofs. The first is His saying: ﴿Is then He who creates like one who does not create?﴾ [al-Naḥl: 17], for when it is established that God is the Creator of all existing things, it is impossible for any of them to be His partner. The second is His saying: ﴿If there had been in them gods other than God, they would have been ruined﴾ [al-Anbiyā': 22]. The third is His saying: ﴿Say: If there had been with Him gods as they say, they would have sought a way to the Possessor of the Throne﴾ [al-Isrā': 42]. The fourth is His saying: ﴿And there was not with Him any god; otherwise, each god would have taken away what he created, and some of them would have overcome others﴾ [al-Mu'minūn: 91]. We have explained these verses in their places, and we have discussed the reality of tawhid (oneness of God) in His saying: ﴿And your God is one God﴾ [al-Baqarah: 163].

﴿God, the Eternal Refuge﴾. There are three opinions concerning the meaning of al-ṣamad (the Eternal Refuge). The first: al-ṣamad is the one to whom one turns in affairs, that is, one who is sought for refuge. The second: He neither eats nor drinks, as in His saying: ﴿He feeds but is not fed﴾ [al-An'ām: 14]. The third: He has no hollow interior. The first is what is meant here according to the more apparent view. Ibn 'Atiyya preferred it, because God is the originator of existing things and by Him they subsist. They are in need of Him, that is, they turn to Him, since they cannot subsist by themselves. Our shaykh, the professor Abū Ja'far ibn al-Zubayr, also preferred it, because this meaning occurs in the Qur'an wherever the negation of offspring from God is mentioned, as in His saying concerning Maryam: ﴿And they say: God has taken a son﴾, followed by His saying: ﴿There is none in the heavens and the earth but that he comes to the Most Merciful as a servant﴾ [Maryam: 93]; and His saying: ﴿The Originator of the heavens and the earth: how could He have a son?﴾ [al-An'ām: 101]; and His saying: ﴿And they say: God has taken a son. Glory be to Him! Rather, to Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth﴾ [al-Baqarah: 116]. Likewise, it is mentioned here together with His saying ﴿He neither begets nor is begotten﴾, as a proof for the negation of offspring. Al-Zamakhshari said: ṣamad is of the form faʻal in the sense of mafʻūl (passive), because He is the one sought in needs.
